summary: A status report listing the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations. It collected in one place the numbers that protocols agreed to share and replaced earlier editions. It is now historic, and was itself replaced by RFC 1010.

eli5.summary: Many machines need to agree that certain numbers mean certain things, like a phone book. This memo was one edition of that phone book.

questions: where were protocol numbers listed in 1986
subtitle: The November 1986 edition of the Internet's master list of assigned protocol numbers, ports and addresses.

tldr.problem: Many protocols need numbers and keywords that every implementation agrees on, such as network numbers, IP protocol numbers and port numbers. Without one list, assignments would collide.
tldr.mechanism: This memo collects the currently assigned values from several series of numbers in one status report, with a contact person for new assignments. It covers network numbers, version, protocol and port numbers, ARP and Ethernet values, Telnet options and more.
tldr.outcome: It is a snapshot, not a protocol. It is now Historic: RFC 1010 obsoleted it, and RFC 997 updated it.

today: RFC 990 is Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 1010 and updated by RFC 997, so its tables are a 1986 snapshot, not a current registry.

sections.title: What the Memo Is
sections.content:
RFC 990 is an official status report on the numbers used in protocols in the ARPA-Internet community. It documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations, and says it will be updated periodically.

Assignments were handled by one person, Joyce Reynolds, and anyone developing a protocol that needs a link, socket, port, protocol or network number was asked to contact her. The memo obsoletes a long list of earlier RFCs (including RFC 960) and three IENs.

Each entry carries a bracketed reference at the right margin. The number cites a document in the memo's document list and the letters cite the responsible person.
sections.eli5: One person kept the master list, so everyone who needed a new number asked her instead of picking one at random.

sections.title: How Numbers Are Written
sections.content:
Internet protocol documents express numbers in decimal and picture data in big-endian order: fields are described left to right, with the most significant octet on the left. When a multi-octet quantity is transmitted, the most significant octet goes first.

In a bit diagram, the bit labelled 0 is the most significant bit. The memo's example is the octet 10101010, which is 170 in decimal.
sections.eli5: It is like agreeing to always write the biggest digit of a number first, so everyone reads 170 the same way.

sections.title: Network Numbers and Address Classes
sections.content:
IP uses a 32-bit address divided into a network part and a local part. The memo describes classes: class A has a 7-bit network number and a 24-bit local address; class B has a 14-bit network number and a 16-bit local address; class C has a 21-bit network number and an 8-bit local address. Class D is a multicast address, and class E (leading bits 1-1-1-1) is reserved.

Addresses are written in dotted decimal, for example 10.3.0.52. Each listed network is tagged R, D, G or C for Research, Defense, Government (non-defense) or Commercial. Networks marked with an asterisk are independent networks that must apply separately to interconnect with the ARPA-Internet or DDN-Internet.

Special addresses: zero means 'this', as in this network, all ones means 'all', as in all hosts, and class A network 127 is the loopback function. A datagram sent to a network 127 address should loop back inside the host and never appear on any network.
sections.eli5: An address has two parts, like a street and a house number. Different classes split the address into a bigger street part or a bigger house part.

sections.title: Protocol, Port and Other Parameter Tables
sections.content:
The core tables cover values that protocols look up constantly. The IP version field is 4 bits wide (version 4 is IP). The IP Protocol field is 8 bits (for example 1 is ICMP, 6 is TCP and 17 is UDP).

Ports name the ends of logical connections. A service contact port, also called the well-known port, is where a server waits for unknown callers. Examples in the list: 21 for FTP control, 23 for Telnet, 25 for SMTP, 53 for the domain name server. The same assignments are used with UDP where possible.

The memo also lists autonomous system numbers (a 16-bit field in EGP), Domain System class values, ARPANET logical addresses and link numbers, Ethernet type numbers, ARP parameters, public data network numbers, Telnet options, official machine, system, protocol and terminal type names, and a numbered list of documents.
sections.eli5: Each service sits at a numbered door on the computer. Everyone knows which doors certain services use, so visitors know which one to knock on.

sections.title: Dividing Up the Address Space
sections.content:
Appendix A shows how network numbers in classes A, B and C are allocated among Research, Defense, Government and Commercial uses. For class A, the allocations are 8, 24, 24 and 94 networks, plus the reserved addresses 0 and 127, for a total of 128.

Identifiers are not allocated by simple partition but by specific assignment, so an experimental network that becomes operational need not be renumbered. Its identifier can move between categories as long as the number used by each category stays within the stated limits. Protocol identifiers, port numbers, link numbers, version numbers and option identifiers are shared by all four communities.
sections.eli5: The numbers were shared out between four groups, and if a project moved from one group to another it could keep its number.
